title: Joel Spolsky, Things You Should Never Do: Rewriting the Code from Scratch
summary: Joel Spolsky's essay: rewriting a working codebase from scratch discards hard-won bug fixes and hands years to competitors.

assertions.quote: When you throw away code and start from scratch, you are throwing away all that knowledge, all those collected bug fixes, years of programming work.

verdicts.note: Netscape, Borland and similar cases support it, but successful rewrites exist, so the harm depends on scale and context.

assertions.quote: It's harder to read code than to write it.

verdicts.note: Comprehension consumes most maintenance effort in studies, supporting the premise; the inference about misjudging old code is plausible but untested.

assertions.quote: Even fairly major architectural changes can be done without throwing away the code.

verdicts.note: Incremental re-architecture is widely practiced and documented, but some structural changes are impractical without large rewrites.

assertions.quote: there is absolutely no reason to believe that you are going to do a better job than you did the first time

verdicts.note: Second-system effects are documented, but a rewrite with clearer requirements can succeed.

assertions.quote: When optimizing for speed, 1% of the work gets you 99% of the bang.

verdicts.note: Hotspot concentration is a well-established profiling finding; the exact ratio varies.
